Pattern testing and choke care

To see what your choke really does, you shoot at a pattern plate: a large steel sheet that is painted or greased so the pellets leave marks. A big sheet of paper, about 1 × 1 m, also works. Do this only at a ground that has such a plate, and with the staff's permission.

To check gun fit you shoot from close range, about 15 m (16 yards): what matters there is where the centre of the pattern is. To judge the choke itself the distance is longer, classically 35 m or 40 yards (about 36.6 m). On paper you draw a circle 75–76 cm across around the densest part and count the pellet holes inside it. Then compare that number with the number of pellets in the cartridge (roughly 350–400 for 28 g of No. 7½; see Shot size).

Roughly, at that distance cylinder puts about 40% of the shot in the circle, improved cylinder about 50%, modified about 60%, improved modified about 65%, and full 70% or more. The figures depend on the cartridge, so your own gun and cartridge may give different results.

Tip: One shot proves little: patterns vary noticeably even with identical cartridges. Fire at least 3–5 shots for each combination. Look at evenness too: a good pattern is even, without big holes and without a dense blob in the middle.

  1. After shooting, unscrew the chokes with the choke key.
  2. Clean them inside and out with solvent and a brush, and wipe the thread in the muzzle.
  3. Before screwing them back in, put a thin layer of choke grease on the thread: it prevents rust and stops the choke from seizing.

Check that chokes are tight before each session, because shooting can slowly loosen them. Screw them in fully with the key, but without excessive force.

Safety: Never fire a multichoke gun without a choke, or with a choke that is only half screwed in. The shot and the wad can damage the thread in the muzzle, and the repair is expensive. Keep spare chokes in a separate case so they do not get lost.

Key points

  • Patterns are checked on a plate: fit at about 15 m (16 yards), chokes at 35 m or 40 yards.
  • Count the share of shot in a 75–76 cm circle; fire 3–5 shots.
  • Clean chokes after shooting and grease the threads with choke grease.
  • Check that chokes are tight before each session.
  • Never fire a multichoke gun without a choke.

Did you know?

After each shot the pattern plate is painted or greased again, with a roller or brush, so that the next marks do not mix with the previous ones.

Check yourself · 3 questions

  1. Why should you not fire a multichoke gun without a choke?

    1. It is banned only in competitions
    2. Shot and wad can damage the muzzle thread
    3. The gun will not fire at all then
    4. The pattern becomes far too tight
    Answer

    Shot and wad can damage the muzzle thread

    Without a choke the thread is exposed, and the shot and wad can damage it.

  2. At what classic distance is a choke's pattern judged?

    1. 5 m (about 5½ yards)
    2. 15 m (about 16 yards)
    3. 35 m or 40 yards (about 37 m)
    4. 80 m (about 87 yards)
    Answer

    35 m or 40 yards (about 37 m)

    The share of shot in a 75–76 cm circle is classically counted at 35 m or 40 yards.

  3. How many shots should you fire to judge a pattern?

    1. At least 3–5 for each pair
    2. One shot is enough for this
    3. Exactly two, one per barrel
    4. A hundred, on the same day
    Answer

    At least 3–5 for each pair

    Patterns vary from shot to shot, so you need a series for each gun, choke and cartridge.
